title: Load testing and extreme scenarios
subtitle: Designing a test for the worst day, not for an average day multiplied by two
whyItMatters: Most load tests measure what the system is good at and miss what brings it down, because they are designed by multiplying normal traffic rather than by asking how it fails.
openingQuestion: You are designing a load test. Where do you start?
openingOptions: From how the system has failed before
From current traffic multiplied by some factor to see how much headroom there is
From next year's projected load, plus a margin for the busiest periods of the year
From the hardware limits, so you know the theoretical ceiling the system could reach
explanation: Multiplying traffic is the most natural approach and it tests exactly one direction: can the system take more. Real incidents rarely have that shape - they come from misshapen load, from a dependency slowing down, or from data of an unusual shape. The incident history is the only list describing the shapes that have actually brought this system down.

diagram.label: Incident history: how it has failed
Rebuild each shape as a test
Add scenarios that have not happened but could
Measure the time to come back, not just the breaking point

realWorldExample.company: Survived five times the peak, fell over at normal load
realWorldExample.description: A system passed a test at five times peak traffic and was approved for release. The first incident came at ordinary load, when a dependency responded about two seconds slower than usual. Waiting connections piled up, memory filled, and the system fell over. The test was never wrong - it had simply never tried that shape, because it was designed by multiplication.

sections.text: A load test answers how much the system can take. An extreme scenario answers a different and more important question: how it fails, and how long it takes to come back.
Four shapes worth more than a multiplier

items: A dependency slowing down without dying - the shape that causes most collapses and is rarely tested
Load arriving inside a few seconds instead of spread out, for instance after a notification send
Data of unusual shape: one user holding a thousand times the average amount of data
Part of the infrastructure disappearing mid-flight, with the rest having to carry it without time to scale

sections.text: The first shape deserves attention because it is counterintuitive. A dependency that dies outright means the system gets an error immediately and can handle it; a dependency that slows down means every request waits, resources stay held, and the system dies of exhausted connections rather than of any error at all. This is why a maximum wait time matters more than most other settings.
Measure the time to come back, not just the breaking point

Most tests stop at finding the threshold where the system starts to fail, and that is half an answer. The other half is what happens next: does it recover on its own once load drops, or does it stay in the broken state until somebody restarts it. Those two behaviours differ in severity far more than they differ in threshold.

sections.label: A system that does not recover doubles every incident
sections.text: If load exceeds the threshold for three minutes and the system needs human intervention to work again, then every short traffic spike becomes a long incident. A test finds this with one extra step: after forcing the system to break, drop the load back to normal and watch. That step costs five minutes and is rarely in the script.

left.label: Testing by shape
left.text: Rebuild the ways this system has failed, plus a few that have not happened. The result says how it fails and how long it takes to return.

right.label: Testing by multiplier
right.text: Normal traffic times five. The result is a threshold number, and it predicts none of the real incidents.

sections.text: A test run once before release is only true for that version. The system changes every week, and most changes shift the shape of how it handles load in ways nobody anticipates. Rerunning on a schedule, even one scenario a month, is worth more than one comprehensive test and then nothing.

lines: Real incidents rarely have the shape of normal traffic multiplied up.
A dependency that slows down is more dangerous than one that dies outright.

quiz.question: Why is designing a load test by multiplying traffic not enough?
options: Because running it consumes a large amount of infrastructure resources for the duration
Because real incidents rarely have that shape
Because the multiplier is chosen arbitrarily, so results are not comparable between runs
Because it only measures the compute path and not storage or data transfer
quiz.explanation: Multiplying tests one direction: can it take more. Real incidents come from misshapen load, a dependency slowing down, or unusual data - three shapes an even multiplier never produces.

quiz.question: Why is a dependency that slows down more dangerous than one that dies?
options: Because automatic retry logic multiplies the requests being sent to the slow dependency
Because the system cannot detect that anything is wrong at all in that situation
Because every request waits, so resources stay held until they run out
Because the delay usually grows gradually, making the moment to intervene hard to pick
quiz.explanation: Dying outright means the system gets an error immediately and handles it. Slowing down means there is no error to handle, only connections held longer - and the system dies of exhausted connections rather than of anything that got logged.

quiz.question: Which step is often missing from the test script and costs five minutes to add?
options: Comparing this run's results against the results of the most recent previous run
Capturing the full logs throughout the duration of the test run itself
Running the test at several load levels to find exactly where degradation begins
Dropping load back to normal and watching whether it recovers on its own
quiz.explanation: Most tests stop at the breaking point, which is half an answer. A system that does not recover by itself turns every short spike into a long incident, and that is a far bigger difference than a few percent on the threshold.

quiz.question: What is the best source for designing test scenarios?
options: The incident history of this system itself
Published material on the failure patterns that commonly affect systems of this kind
The experience of other teams running systems with a similar architecture in the company
Performance measurements taken in the test environment during recent releases
quiz.explanation: The other three are all useful for adding scenarios that have not happened. Incident history is different in kind: it is the only list describing shapes that have genuinely brought down this system, with its architecture and its dependencies.

quiz.question: Why is one comprehensive test before release not enough?
options: Because results from a test environment do not carry over to production conditions
Because the system changes weekly and each change shifts how it handles load
Because a comprehensive test takes so long that it gets cut under schedule pressure
Because actual load after release is usually very different from what was tested
quiz.explanation: A test result is a statement about one specific version. After ten releases that statement describes a system that no longer exists, so one scenario rerun monthly is worth more than one thorough test and then nothing.

keyTakeaways: Real incidents rarely have the shape of normal traffic multiplied up
A dependency that slows down is more dangerous than one that dies
Measure the time to come back, not only the breaking point
Incident history gives scenarios matched to this system's own architecture

practicePrompt.question: A dependency adds 2 seconds, the system has 200 connections, each request holds one. At 150 requests per second, how long until connections run out?
options: About 1.3 seconds
2 seconds
It does not run out, because each connection is released as soon as the dependency replies
About 30 seconds (= dividing the connection count by the delay rather than by the arrival rate)
practicePrompt.explanation: 150 requests per second each holding a connection for 2 seconds means held connections grow by 150 every second. 200 divided by 150 is about 1.3 seconds to exhaustion. Two seconds of added delay is enough to bring down a system nowhere near any processing limit.

summary.keyIdea: Test the shapes that have broken the system, not a multiplier
summary.commonMistake: Stopping the test at the breaking point without checking recovery
summary.action: Take your three most recent incident write-ups and turn each into a test scenario.

application.title: Four minimum scenarios
application.message: A dependency slowing down. Load arriving in seconds. One user with a thousand times the data. Losing part of the infrastructure mid-flight.
application.secondary: After each one, drop the load back to normal and see whether the system returns on its own.
